You bet…in every sense of those words. The themes they mentioned…psychological collapse, personal struggle, and social decay never felt so alive as they do here. Some of the material reminded me of the darker, fringe electronic music of my youth, but it was twisted with poison, mutilated with darkness, and tortured with anguish, and an almost suffocating sense of despair. Traveling Without Moving Active Intersection I always appreciate an album that goes as much into a story or a theme as it does the music, because pairing the two can make for a fulfilling listening experience. That is what we have here. The music is mostly smooth and gentle, a little dark, and just dangerous enough to keep you on your toes matching the story. This album has style, substance, and character, and I recommend it to anyone who wrestles at times with trying to find the definition of life. More importantly, it’s also confident, and that kind of thing usually comes from a seasoned band with a few albums in their inventory. The right mix of ingredients is definitely here. Aion’s Light Blood & Sun This album was definitely outside of my wheelhouse, and I’m surprised how much I enjoyed it. Worldwide. 24/7. October 18, 2026 On The Turntable Close The Clientele :: Suburban Light It can be difficult to verbalize exactly what autumnal records are capable of eliciting. One thing is undeniable: October and November are the months for The Clientele’s 2000 debut album Suburban Light . Perhaps most impressive, the uninitiated would never detect that such an accomplished record was comprised mostly of a smattering of the band’s earlier 7″ singles from the years prior. Though ideal for any season, the record is an impeccable collection of reveries that paint a viscerally evocative picture of sundown strolls with scattered leaves underfoot. Read More Spotify Apple Music Tidal Close Mark Hollis :: Mark Hollis The quietly revolutionary Talk Talk singer made one final album before calling it quits: his self-titled solo album debut, from 1998. While often overshadowed by the majestic experimentation of his former project’s late work, Mark Hollis harbors its own secrets and surprises, while building upon the work those albums began. As a final testament, it’s a fitting paradox, full of roaring silences and whispering explosions, a collection of whisper-thin abstractions that have been annealed into something durable and concrete. One of the era’s great young singjays, Boyo moves between vocal and dub across twelve tracks, his delivery drifting over heavyweight riddims before disappearing into the mix. Full of swagger yet mellow and unhurried, he rides the bass-heavy arrangements through a thick haze of echo and reverb. Read More Erasmo Carlos :: Carlos, Erasmo (1971) Posted on November 27, 2026 November 26, 2026 At once freezing and tropical, airy and baroque, swinging with dizzying freedom between electric and acoustic, fuzzed-out and bare, wound-up and laid-back. It’s a little chimera of garage-soul MPB: it bites, it grooves, it drives, it eventually rests. Now reissued by Vampisoul less than a decade after Light in the Attic’s historic 2017 reedition, it arrives like a second knock on a door that, half a century later, is still only ajar. David Axelrod :: S/T Posted on November 27, 2026 November 21, 2026 In 2000, cinematic composer and jazz producer David Axelrod was invited to record a new album by British label Mo’ Wax (DJ Shadow, Parsley Sound). The self-titled record was built upon the discovery of rare acetates that were to be the final installment of Axelrod’s shapeshifting sixties trilogy with the Electric Prunes such as the Latin-sung, psychedelic Mass in F Minor. This eponymous record is starkly referential to all of the various stages of Axelrod’s iconoclast career, from his catalogue becoming an endless sample trove for hip-hop architects to reconnecting with sixties collaborators like soul singer Lou Rawls. Spike Fuck :: Evidence Posted on November 26, 2026 November 26, 2026 Spike Fuck lives in restless extremity. The Australian art punk provocateur has tried all the vices—heroin, cigarettes, religion, abstinence—one by one. For a period in the teens, he transitioned medically, recording and performing as a woman, before changing back again in the 2020s. He lived in a monastery at one point. None of these experiments gave him what he was looking for, so he discarded them just as easily as he picked them up. Post-punk, synth weirdness, crooked outsider pop, shadowy electronics, dubby rhythms, warped grooves. 34.1090° N, 118.2334° W Late November :: Autumnal Britfolk Instrumentals (1968-1981) Posted on November 25, 2026 November 21, 2026 The shadows are lengthening, the leaves are falling, the air is getting crisp. That’s right, we’re heading into the latter days of autumn. Maybe the best time of year? One of them, anyway. The season demands a soundtrack, and for some reason, the loosely organized britfolk genre is perfect for these days. So here’s an hour’s worth of instrumentals from the late 1960s to the early 1980s, when giants walked the earth. Trad melodies and rhythms abound, but there are plenty of left-turns, mostly thanks to dedicated iconoclasts like John Martyn, Davey Graham and Michael Chapman. Grab a pint of something dark and rich and settle in. Transmissions :: Beth Orton Posted on November 25, 2026 November 25, 2026 This week on the show, we’re presenting the penultimate episode of our 12th season. And we’ve saved a tremendous talk for this second to last installment: our guest is singer/songwriter Beth Orton. In the mid-’90s, she emerged as a purveyor of electronic folk, working with artists like William Orbit, The Chemical Brothers, and Four Tet. Her latest is The Ground Above. Reviewing it for Aquarium Drunkard, Kyle Lemmon described it as “a free-flowing mixture of electronic funk, spirit walking jazz, and ambient folk.” Miles Davis: Copenhagen Live 1969 Posted on November 24, 2026 November 21, 2026 Miles Davis’ 1969 live ensemble existed in a parallel timeline alongside his studio work – greasing his audience for a future for which they were wholly unprepared. A new 2LP set, Copenhagen Live 1969 , captures the band at its peak, stress-testing then-unreleased Bitches Brew material, tearing it down and reassembling it into some of the most far-out, formless music of Miles’ career. The Lagniappe Sessions :: Shane Butler Posted on November 24, 2026 November 22, 2026 Shane Butler’s first solo record, Heavy Debt , is due next month, and for this Lagniappe Session he’s pulled together three songs that have been rattling around for a long time. Fugazi’s “I’m So Tired,” a song he first encountered as a kid watching skate videos, Shoes’ homemade pop and a 1979 Soft Boys’ nugget. Frank Black :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview Posted on November 24, 2026 November 24, 2026 In 2025, Pixies leader Frank Black took to the road to celebrate the 30th anniversary of his 1994 sophomore LP Teenager of the Year with the same cast of players who recorded the original album. A sprawling double album, it’s held together with the same kind of ramshackle logic that makes The Beatles’ The White Album or The Clash’s London Calling work. Recently, Aquarium Drunkard caught up with Black to discuss revisiting the album. Along the way, he revealed details about a Pixies record in the works, UFOs, the paranormal, and explained his vision of a future rock & roll cult where artists like The Feelies are elevated to the status of saints. Fine :: Jazz Dreams Posted on November 23, 2026 November 23, 2026 For all the creativity Copenhagen’s avant-pop scene can offer, a lot of it had started to hang on its own clichés. Who knew it could be recharged by a blasé attitude and a good old dose of harmonic complexity? Fine’s Jazz Dreams is full of the kind of drowsy virtuosity that once again justifies the hype over that scene’s prolific output; it’s as if you were inhabiting the fantasies of a conservatory student who fell asleep in counterpoint class. Tía Rosa :: Thirteen Automatic Dreams Posted on November 23, 2026 November 23, 2026 Via Mexico City, Thirteen Automatic Dreams is the thrillingly comfy new record by Tía Rosa. Here is some minimalist kosmische with a Latin pop sensibility, a bridge between the noisy regularity of Neu! and the sugared melancholy of balada romántica. It all plays like a lost soundtrack to the Nevada desert of the Nocilla Trilogy , where shoes hang from a lonely poplar, or like Stereolab is being collectively hallucinated from one of those little Durango towns where Jodorowsky liked to film his deranged acid westerns. Sunday Mourners :: A-Rhythm Absolute Posted on November 23, 2026 November 21, 2026 Skirting the edges of canonical post-punk, the debut record by four piece Sunday Mourners is a gripping, youthful art-rock explosion. There are distinct flashes tapping into Chairs Missing -era jagged melodicism here, VU at their most intractable jamming there (the twelve minute “Darling” a prime example). Above all, A-Rhythm Absolute is a downright lively listen, hitting all of the spirited guitar-centric benchmarks to make the listener a reinvigorated believer in the state of such a modern landscape. Happy Thanksgiving :: Doug Sahm And Friends – Austin, TX 1972 Posted on November 21, 2026 November 21, 2026 Tradition runs rampant around Thanksgiving: generations of old recipes, football, Alice’s Restaurant, and, of course, a parade of balloons shutting down NYC. What else do you need? If you thought you were covered in the Thanksgiving tradition department, we did too…until a few years ago, when someone blew the dust off a long lost tape — Doug Sahm’s Thanksgiving Jam.
